content: Genital herpes is a sexually transmitted viral infection that affects the skin or mucous membranes of the genital area. Many individuals infected with herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) may not experience noticeable symptoms or may mistake mild symptoms for other conditions, such as insect bites. However, when symptoms do occur during the initial outbreak, they can be severe. Systemic symptoms during the first outbreak may include: Loss of appetite. Fever. General malaise or a feeling of being unwell. Muscle aches, particularly in the lower back, buttocks, thighs, or knees. Genital symptoms often involve the development of small, painful blisters filled with clear or straw-colored fluid. These blisters may appear: In women: on the outer vaginal lips (labia), inside the vagina, on the cervix, around the anus, or on the thighs and buttocks. In men: on the penis, scrotum, around the anus, or on the thighs and buttocks. In both sexes: on the tongue, mouth, eyes, gums, lips, fingers, or other areas of the body. Before the blisters form, individuals may experience sensations such as tingling, burning, itching, or localized pain at the site where the blisters will develop. Once the blisters rupture, they leave behind shallow, painful ulcers that eventually crust over and heal within 7 to 14 days or longer. Additional symptoms that may occur include: Swollen and tender lymph nodes in the groin during an outbreak. Painful urination. Vaginal discharge in women, or in rare cases, difficulty emptying the bladder, which may require catheterization. Subsequent outbreaks can occur weeks or months after the initial episode. These recurrent outbreaks are generally less severe and shorter in duration. Over time, the frequency of outbreaks may decrease. However, once infected, the virus remains in the body, residing in nerve cells in a dormant state (latency). Reactivation of the virus can occur at any time, triggered by factors such as: Fatigue. Irritation in the genital area. Menstruation. Physical or emotional stress. Trauma. The frequency of recurrent outbreaks varies widely, ranging from once a year to nearly continuous symptoms. Recurrent infections tend to be milder and shorter in men compared to women. Genital herpes is caused by two types of herpes simplex viruses: 1. Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), which is the most common cause of genital herpes. 2. Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), which more commonly causes oral herpes (cold sores) but can also cause genital herpes through oral-genital contact. The virus is transmitted through direct contact with the skin, mouth, or genital secretions of an infected individual. Transmission is most likely during active outbreaks when visible sores or blisters are present. However, the virus can also be spread when no symptoms or visible sores are present, as the infected person may still shed the virus asymptomatically. This makes it possible for individuals who are unaware of their infection to transmit the virus to others. Genital HSV-2 infections are more prevalent in women (approximately 1 in 4 women) than in men (approximately 1 in 8 men). It is important to seek medical attention if you experience symptoms of genital herpes, such as fever, headache, vomiting, or systemic symptoms during or after an outbreak. Additionally, consult a healthcare provider if you are unable to urinate. Diagnosis of genital herpes can be confirmed through laboratory tests, particularly during the first outbreak or in pregnant women with symptoms. Diagnostic methods include: Viral culture: Fluid from a blister or open sore is tested for the presence of the herpes simplex virus. This test is most effective during the initial outbreak and typically provides results within 2-3 days. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR): This highly accurate test detects small amounts of viral DNA in fluid from a blister. Blood tests: Although there is no cure for genital herpes, antiviral medications can help manage the condition. These medications, such as acyclovir, famciclovir, and valacyclovir, can reduce pain and discomfort during outbreaks and promote faster healing of sores. They are most effective during the first outbreak but can also be used for recurrent episodes. For individuals with frequent outbreaks, daily suppressive therapy with antiviral medications can reduce the frequency and severity of outbreaks and lower the risk of transmitting the virus to others. Pregnant women with genital herpes may be treated with antiviral medications during the final month of pregnancy to minimize the risk of an outbreak during delivery. If an outbreak occurs at the time of delivery, a cesarean section (C-section) is recommended to prevent transmission of the virus to the newborn. Side effects of antiviral medications may include: Fatigue. Headache. Nausea and vomiting. Rash. Seizures. Tremors. Home care for herpes sores includes: Avoiding tight or synthetic clothing, such as nylon underwear or pantyhose. Instead, wear loose-fitting cotton garments. Gently cleansing the affected area with soap and water. Taking warm baths to relieve pain, followed by keeping the blisters dry. If a bacterial infection develops in one of the sores, consult a healthcare provider to determine if antibiotics are necessary. The prognosis for genital herpes varies. While some individuals may never experience another outbreak after the initial episode, others may have frequent recurrences. Triggers for outbreaks include fatigue, general illness, immunosuppression, menstruation, stress, and trauma to the affected area. In individuals with normal immune systems, genital herpes is typically a localized and bothersome condition but is rarely life-threatening. However, complications can arise, particularly in pregnant women and immunocompromised individuals. Pregnant women with active genital herpes at the time of delivery may transmit the virus to their newborn, leading to severe complications such as brain infection (meningitis or encephalitis), chronic skin infection, developmental delays, or even death. The risk of transmission is highest during a primary infection acquired during pregnancy. Severe herpes infections involving the brain, eyes, esophagus, liver, spinal cord, or lungs can occur in individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with AIDS, undergoing chemotherapy, or taking high doses of steroids. Additionally, individuals with active herpes infections are at an increased risk of acquiring HIV if exposed. Preventing genital herpes involves avoiding sexual contact with infected individuals, particularly during active outbreaks. Consistent and correct use of latex condoms during all sexual activity significantly reduces the risk of transmission. However, animal membrane condoms (e.g., sheepskin) are ineffective, as the virus can pass through them. Female condoms have also been shown to reduce the risk of transmission. Individuals with genital herpes should inform their sexual partners about their condition, even if they are asymptomatic. Experimental vaccines for herpes are under development but are not yet widely available.
